title: Plasterer's apprentice and hearing John Marrero
summary: Family trades were plastering and bricklaying; at 16 he apprenticed as a plasterer until hearing John Marrero decided him on the banjo.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Can you tell us anything else about your family? Did your father favor you?

Oh no, no indeed. No indeed, man, no indeed. You see, my father was a plasterer. And my uncle was a bricklayer, and my grandfather was a plasterer. And it was just the customs of the Creoles that nobody was supposed to break away from nothing. If he was a plasterer, then I was supposed to be a plasterer. Well, when I got to be around 16 years old, they took me, him and Sam Augustin, which was Johnny St. Cyr's stepfather. I went to work with them as a plasterer's apprentice, getting $1.60 a day. That's what it was. And I mean, it was a grind. It was really rough. Ain't no hours. Just wait till he said get through. So, I mean, I just kept on that, and I mean, that was beginning to get the best of me, and I mean, the work was really hard. And I went out to dance one night with my cousin Margaret and I heard, John Marrera play a banjo, and that was it. He couldn't have got me up with a 10-foot pull to 45 from there, or I'd have made up my mind I was going to play a banjo.
